cases.title: The 15,000-Volt Craft Table
cases.subtitle: Why salvaged microwave transformers turn dry wooden handles into live copper wires—and why grabbing your friend makes you link number two.
cases.looksLike: A trendy backyard wood-burning craft
cases.actuallyIs: An unshielded 15,000-volt electric chair
cases.abstract: Wood is an insulator—right up until a salvaged microwave transformer punches electrons straight through its cellular structure. Two fatal home-workshop cases show why wooden dowels fail, why AC locks your fist around the wire, and the single bystander rule that keeps a rescuer alive.
cases.goldenRule: Never touch an electrocuted victim or workbench; cut the main breaker or wall plug first, then start CPR and grab an AED.
cases.episodeTitle: How Garage Voltage, Tire Blasts and Positional Traps Kill

cases.title: The IED Parked in Your Driveway
cases.subtitle: Commercial truck tires inflate to 120 psi and burst past 260—unleashing the same primary blast wave physics as a roadside bomb.
cases.looksLike: Topping off a flat tire on a Tuesday
cases.actuallyIs: Standing 50 cm from a pneumatic fragmentation grenade
cases.abstract: When fatigued steel cords fail silently along a truck sidewall, a 'zipper' burst unleashes a shockwave strong enough to shear major vessels and dislocate the skull from the spine. Learn the blast-standoff rules and why surviving with just ear bleeding still demands a trauma CT.
cases.goldenRule: Use a steel restraining cage and a clip-on remote chuck from at least 2.5 meters away—never face a commercial sidewall.
cases.episodeTitle: How Garage Voltage, Tire Blasts and Positional Traps Kill

cases.title: When Furniture and Gravity Hold a Grudge
cases.subtitle: Ottoman storage beds with tired gas struts and 40-cm tank hatches prove you can suffocate in 20.8% oxygen without anything touching your throat.
cases.looksLike: Reaching into a storage bed or farm tank
cases.actuallyIs: Class 5 mechanical leverage against your diaphragm
cases.abstract: Lean past your hips into a smooth hatch or reach near the hinge fulcrum of a sagging ottoman mattress, and biomechanics turn hostile in seconds. Here is how diaphragmatic splinting and inverted venous overload work—and the dead-simple leverage trick to prevent both.
cases.goldenRule: Always access ottoman beds from the foot end with a rigid prop bar, and never lean head-first into a hatch without a capable standby.
cases.episodeTitle: How Garage Voltage, Tire Blasts and Positional Traps Kill

cases.title: The Air That Came Along for the Ride
cases.subtitle: Solid CO₂ sitting quietly in a closed car sublimates into an invisible heavy blanket that can knock out the driver—and stun the heart.
cases.looksLike: Bringing frozen groceries home in a cooler
cases.actuallyIs: Replacing cabin oxygen with heavy CO₂ vapor
cases.abstract: Dry ice does not melt into a puddle; it expands directly into dense carbon dioxide gas that pools inside closed cabins and triggers hypoxia plus stress cardiomyopathy. Learn how to transport it safely—and how rescuers avoid collapsing next to the car door.
cases.goldenRule: Never carry dry ice in an occupied passenger cabin or sealed container; use vented packaging in a separate, ventilated cargo compartment, and call 911 rather than leaning in to rescue.
cases.episodeTitle: The Air That Came Along for the Ride — Dry-Ice Carbon Dioxide Sublimation in an Enclosed Vehicle Associated With Reversible Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy — Rescuer Safety & Safe Transport Physics

cases.title: The Cut That Was Smaller Than the Injury
cases.subtitle: A high-pressure washer leaves a harmless-looking pinhole on the skin—while silently jetting fluid deep down tendon sheaths.
cases.looksLike: A tiny sting you can slap a Band-Aid on
cases.actuallyIs: High-pressure hydraulic tissue dissection
cases.abstract: High-pressure injection injuries are famous ER traps because the entry dot looks trivial during the first few painless hours while deep compartments swell and die. Waiting overnight can cost a finger or limb.
cases.goldenRule: Treat any high-pressure washer, paint-sprayer, or grease-gun skin puncture as an immediate ER surgical emergency—even if it barely bleeds.
cases.episodeTitle: The Cut That Was Smaller Than the Injury — High-Pressure Washer Micro-Puncture Injecting Fluid Along Tendon Sheaths — Compartmental Biomechanics & Emergent Surgical Decompression

cases.title: The Puncture That Looked Too Small
cases.subtitle: A pneumatic nail-gun chest wound with zero symptoms and a reassuring first X-ray—until deeper imaging reveals what sits next to the heart.
cases.looksLike: A ricochet scratch that stopped hurting
cases.actuallyIs: An occult thoracic projectile near the myocardium
cases.abstract: Pneumatic framing nails travel fast enough to penetrate the chest wall with minimal external bleeding and deceptive stability. Feeling fine for an hour does not clear a nail-gun strike to the torso.
cases.goldenRule: Never pull an embedded nail out yourself, and get cross-sectional trauma evaluation for any nail-gun chest or neck puncture even if you feel fine.
cases.episodeTitle: The Puncture That Looked Too Small — Asymptomatic Pneumatic Nail-Gun Chest Puncture With Normal Vitals & Negative FAST Yet Paracardiac Foreign Body on Contrast CT

cases.title: The Alarm Beyond the Wall
cases.subtitle: Why running a storm generator 'outside' next to a garage door or soffit vent still turns bedrooms into carbon monoxide chambers.
cases.looksLike: Smart hurricane prep with the garage door cracked
cases.actuallyIs: Aerodynamic exhaust siphoning straight indoors
cases.abstract: A 167-case Florida post-storm audit revealed that 'outside under the eaves' or 'in the open garage' is nowhere near far enough when wind eddies pull odorless CO back into living spaces.
cases.goldenRule: Place portable generators at least 20 feet (6 meters) away from doors, windows, and vents—pointed downwind—with battery-backed CO alarms inside.
cases.episodeTitle: The Alarm Beyond the Wall — Post-Storm Portable Generator Exhaust Aerodynamics (167 Florida Cases, 16 Outdoor vs. 16 Garage), Wind-Wake Infiltration, Pulse Oximetry SpO2 Blindness & Battery CO Alarms

cases.title: The Wire Behind the Pain
cases.subtitle: How a stray metal bristle from a backyard grill brush can punch through your small intestine without tasting like metal, making you vomit, or leaving blood in the toilet.
cases.looksLike: A nagging stomach ache with normal bowel movements
cases.actuallyIs: A metal bristle perforating the small bowel into an abscess
cases.abstract: A 51-year-old woman in Denmark had two days of worsening belly pain, zero nausea, normal stool, and zero memory of swallowing anything sharp. Laparoscopy pulled a thin piece of metal wire straight out of her small intestine—exposing why normal stool never proves an intact gut wall.
cases.goldenRule: Ditch metal-bristle grill brushes; if sharp pain hits after eating—or you feel a swallowed wire—skip bread/vomiting tricks and get urgent medical care.
cases.episodeTitle: The Wire Behind the Pain — Unrecalled Wire Bristle Ingestion & Small-Bowel Perforation, High-Attenuation CT Streak Detection & Migrating Abscess Surgery

cases.title: The Lunch That Looked Like an Allergy
cases.subtitle: You aren't suddenly allergic to tuna—warm storage let bacteria convert fish amino acids into a massive, heat-proof dose of histamine.
cases.looksLike: Sudden adult-onset seafood anaphylaxis
cases.actuallyIs: Scombroid histamine poisoning (cooking won't destroy it)
cases.abstract: Peppery-tasting tuna, flushing, hives, pounding headache, and racing pulse minutes after lunch fool patients and ERs alike into diagnosing a lifelong fish allergy. Because histamine is heat-stable, searing a mishandled fillet locks the chemical punch right in.
cases.goldenRule: Spit out tuna, mackerel, or mahi-mahi that tastes metallic or peppery; seek urgent care for breathing trouble, and know antihistamines treat scombroid.
cases.episodeTitle: The Lunch That Looked Like an Allergy — Scombroid Histamine Fish Poisoning, Paris Yellowfin Tuna Outbreak (40 Cases, 39/79 Attack Rate), Heat-Stable Histidine Decarboxylation & Supply-Chain Forensics

cases.title: The Room That Was Not Safe to Finish
cases.subtitle: Mixing household bleach with acid or ammonia turns a tiled bathroom with the door shut into a miniature World War I trench.
cases.looksLike: Double-strength bathroom deep-cleaning
cases.actuallyIs: Generating chlorine or chloramine gas in an unventilated box
cases.abstract: Trying to scrub a stubborn tub by layering two everyday bottles releases corrosive gases that burn airways on contact and can trigger delayed pulmonary edema hours after you step into the hallway.
cases.goldenRule: Never mix bleach with vinegar, toilet-bowl acids, or ammonia; if fumes hit your chest, abandon the room immediately for fresh air and call Poison Control.
cases.episodeTitle: The Room That Was Not Safe to Finish — Household Cleaning-Agent Inhalation Injury, Point-of-Care Lung Ultrasound B-Lines, Delayed Pulmonary Edema Risk & Indoor Evacuation Rules

cases.title: The Herbal Tea That Stole Potassium
cases.subtitle: Real black licorice root blocks a kidney gatekeeper enzyme, tricking your body into dumping potassium until your muscles—and heart—stall.
cases.looksLike: A soothing daily wellness habit
cases.actuallyIs: Apparent mineralocorticoid excess & severe hypokalemia
cases.abstract: Glycyrrhizic acid inside authentic licorice tea and candy shuts down 11β-HSD2 in the kidney, letting ordinary cortisol impersonate aldosterone. Blood pressure spikes while potassium crashes toward paralysis and arrhythmia.
cases.goldenRule: Treat real licorice root (glycyrrhizin) like a blood-pressure drug—never binge it daily, especially with diuretics or hypertension.
cases.episodeTitle: How Licorice Tea Caused Sudden Paralysis

cases.title: Wild Garlic's Lethal Lookalike
cases.subtitle: One spring salad leaf looks identical to ramsons—except autumn crocus packs colchicine, a toxin that freezes cell division solid.
cases.looksLike: Fresh foraged wild garlic pesto
cases.actuallyIs: Colchicine mitotic arrest & multi-organ failure
cases.abstract: Every spring, hikers pick Colchicum autumnale mistaking its leaves for wild garlic. Early GI upset is followed by a treacherous calm—before bone marrow, heart, and kidneys collapse from microtubule arrest.
cases.goldenRule: Never forage wild garlic by leaf shape alone—if a foraged meal triggers severe vomiting/diarrhea, bring leftover leaves straight to the ER immediately.
cases.episodeTitle: Wild Garlic Mistakes and Lethal Colchicine Mitotic Arrest

cases.title: The Leftover Pasta and the Home-Canned Jar
cases.subtitle: Why boiling won't save rice left on the counter overnight—and how low-acid home canning breeds the deadliest biological toxin on Earth.
cases.looksLike: Thrifty meal prep & artisanal pantry jars
cases.actuallyIs: Bacillus cereus cereulide & Clostridium botulinum neurotoxin
cases.abstract: Reheating room-temperature cooked rice kills the bacteria while leaving behind heat-resistant cereulide toxin capable of fulminant liver failure. Meanwhile, bulging or un-pressure-canned low-acid jars hide odorless botulinum toxin.
cases.goldenRule: Refrigerate cooked rice and pasta within 2 hours (never leave overnight on the stove), and discard any bulging, spurting, or improperly pressure-canned jars.
cases.episodeTitle: Home Canned Botulism and Reheated Rice Liver Shock

cases.title: The Fruit That Breaks Your Liver's Hangover Switch (and the Gut That Brews IPA)
cases.subtitle: Why mixing durian with rum jams mitochondrial ALDH2—plus the forensic cases where a patient's own gut microbes beat a DUI charge.
cases.looksLike: Tropical dessert & a cocktail (or a bizarre breathalyzer)
cases.actuallyIs: 70% thiol inactivation of ALDH2 / endogenous yeast fermentation
cases.abstract: Sulfur compounds in durian chemically knock out the enzyme that clears toxic acetaldehyde, turning a modest drink into a brutal flushing crisis—while in rare auto-brewery syndrome, gut yeast turns plain carbs into 200+ mg/dL blood alcohol.
cases.goldenRule: Skip alcohol with durian (especially if you carry an ALDH2 flushing variant), and investigate unexplained 'drunkenness without drinking' via supervised glucose testing.
cases.episodeTitle: Why Southeast Asia Bans Durian on Subways & Why Mixing It With Rum Blocks Liver Enzymes — Subway Bans & Library Gas-Leak Evacuations, Li, Schieberle & Steinhaus's 2-Compound Durian Simulation (Ethyl (2S)-2-Methylbutanoate + 1-pg/L 1-(Ethylsulfanyl)ethane-1-thiol), Teh's 4-Copy Durian MGL Genome Expansion (PDB 1GC0, 2RFV) & Plant L-Ethionine, and Maninang's ~70% Diethyl Disulfide Thiol–Disulfide Inactivation of Cys302–Cys301/303 Inside Human Mitochondrial ALDH2 (PDB 1O01, 3N80)

cases.title: The Toothache That Turned the Blood Chocolate-Brown
cases.subtitle: How an over-the-counter numbing gel quietly rusted a healthy 29-year-old's hemoglobin, why pulse oximeters lie near 85–88%, and the blue dye that reversed it in 15 minutes.
cases.looksLike: A stubborn toothache & a normal heart rate of 70
cases.actuallyIs: 27.4% methemoglobinemia starving tissues of oxygen
cases.abstract: Three days of OTC benzocaine oral gel turned a healthy 29-year-old's skin pale-gray and his blood chocolate-brown. Even on oxygen his fingertip oximeter read 88% and a calculated blood gas printed a soothing 99%—until co-oximetry caught the molecular rust.
cases.goldenRule: Gray or blue skin/lips plus breathlessness after benzocaine gel = stop the product and call 911 immediately; never trust a home pulse oximeter or use it on teething babies.
cases.episodeTitle: The Toothache That Changed the Blood — Over-the-Counter Benzocaine Gel Methemoglobinemia — Chocolate-Brown Arterial Blood, Pulse-Oximeter 85% Plateau Trap, Co-Oximetry & Methylene Blue

cases.title: Medicine Cabinet Roulette: Sleep Aids, Caffeine Rebound & Whippets
cases.subtitle: How OTC antihistamines jam heart sodium channels, why 12 grams of caffeine bounces back *after* dialysis, and how laughing gas rots spinal cord B₁₂.
cases.looksLike: Harmless pharmacy sleep pills, energy powder & party balloons
cases.actuallyIs: Cardiac ion-channel blockade, tissue rebound & B₁₂ oxidation clots
cases.abstract: Common diphenhydramine isn't a gentle sleeping pill at high doses—it blocks cardiac Nav1.5 and hERG channels. Pure caffeine powder can rebound from tissues into cardiac arrest even after dialysis starts clearing blood, and chronic nitrous oxide chemically inactivates vitamin B₁₂ into clots and paralysis.
cases.goldenRule: Never stack OTC sleep aids or scoop pure caffeine powder; treat numbness, gait loss, or chest pain after nitrous use as an urgent B₁₂/PE medical emergency.
cases.episodeTitle: How Everyday Sleep Aids, Caffeine Rebound and Nitrous Turn Lethal

cases.title: The Ten-Year Prescription
cases.subtitle: You took lisinopril without a single side effect for a decade—so why is your tongue suddenly swelling shut at midnight?
cases.looksLike: A weird food allergy you can fix with Benadryl
cases.actuallyIs: ACE-inhibitor bradykinin laryngeal angioedema
cases.abstract: ACE-inhibitor airway swelling can strike out of nowhere ten years into a perfectly stable prescription—and because it's driven by bradykinin rather than histamine, standard allergy pills and even epinephrine often fail to shrink the throat.
cases.goldenRule: Lip, tongue, or throat swelling on an ACE inhibitor (-pril) is an immediate 911 airway emergency—never wait to see if antihistamines kick in.
cases.episodeTitle: The Ten-Year Prescription — Late-Onset Lisinopril Bradykinin Laryngeal Angioedema After Ten Years of Routine Therapy — Stridor Without Lip/Tongue Swelling & Emergent Airway Protection

cases.title: The Cream and the Missing Stress Response
cases.subtitle: Abruptly stopping a potent overused topical steroid cream can leave your adrenal glands asleep right when your body needs cortisol to survive.
cases.looksLike: Just a skin lotion you decided to quit cold turkey
cases.actuallyIs: Secondary adrenal crisis & shock
cases.abstract: Skin absorbs potent topical steroids far better than most patients realize. Long-term heavy application quietly suppresses the brain-adrenal axis—meaning an abrupt stop or minor illness can trigger life-threatening cortisol failure.
cases.goldenRule: Taper long-term high-potency steroid creams under medical guidance, and flag steroid use immediately if severe weakness, vomiting, or dizziness hits.
cases.episodeTitle: The Cream and the Missing Stress Response — Secondary Adrenal Crisis After Abrupt Potent Topical Corticosteroid Withdrawal — Blunted Cortisol Stimulation During Septic Shock & Safe Taper Guidance

cases.title: The Bottle That Wasn't a Feed
cases.subtitle: Why giving plain water—or stretching formula with extra water—can trigger hyponatremic brain swelling and seizures in young infants.
cases.looksLike: Keeping a hot baby hydrated with plain water
cases.actuallyIs: Dilutional hyponatremia & cerebral edema
cases.abstract: Immature infant kidneys cannot dump free water the way adult kidneys do. Plain water bottles or over-diluted formula rapidly drop blood sodium, driving water straight into brain cells until seizures erupt.
cases.goldenRule: Under 6 months, babies need only breast milk or properly measured formula—never plain water or diluted feeds; call 911 immediately for infant lethargy or seizures.
cases.episodeTitle: The Bottle That Wasn't a Feed — Infant Water Intoxication & Hyponatremic Seizures From Bottled/Diluted Feeds — Immature Free-Water Clearance, Non-Osmotic AVP & 3% Saline Rescue

cases.title: The Heart Medicine and the Ketones
cases.subtitle: How SGLT2 pills can trigger full-blown diabetic ketoacidosis while your blood glucose meter prints a completely 'reassuring' normal number.
cases.looksLike: A stomach bug with a totally fine finger-stick sugar
cases.actuallyIs: Euglycemic ketoacidosis
cases.abstract: SGLT2 inhibitors protect hearts and kidneys by peeing out excess glucose—which also masks ketoacidosis by keeping blood sugar deceptively normal while blood acidity climbs toward coma during fasting, illness, or surgery.
cases.goldenRule: On an SGLT2 inhibitor (-flozin), nausea, vomiting, or deep breathing demands a ketone check even if blood sugar looks normal—and ask doctors about pausing before surgery.
cases.episodeTitle: The Heart Medicine and the Ketones — SGLT2-Inhibitor Euglycemic Ketoacidosis in a Non-Diabetic Heart-Failure Patient — Near-Normal Glucose Masking High-Anion-Gap Ketonemia

cases.title: The Mouth That Looked Unhurt
cases.subtitle: Concentrated laundry detergent pods can burn deep into the esophagus and airways while leaving the lips and tongue looking deceptively clean.
cases.looksLike: A kid spat it out and their mouth looks totally pink
cases.actuallyIs: Occult esophageal & airway caustic injury
cases.abstract: A calm-looking mouth does not rule out severe internal chemical burns or sudden airway swelling after biting into a pressurized detergent pod.
cases.goldenRule: Store detergent pods locked high and out of sight; if bitten or swallowed, do NOT induce vomiting—rinse mouth and call Poison Control or 911 immediately.
cases.episodeTitle: The Mouth That Looked Unhurt — Concentrated Laundry Detergent Pod Ingestion With Normal Oral Mucosa Yet Profound Lactic Acidosis, CNS Depression & Airway Edema

cases.title: The Pain That Outlasted the Class
cases.subtitle: Going all-out in your very first indoor spin class can shred thigh muscle fibers so violently that tea-colored urine signals failing kidneys.
cases.looksLike: Hardcore 'earned' leg-day soreness
cases.actuallyIs: Exertional rhabdomyolysis flooding kidneys with myoglobin
cases.abstract: First-session high-resistance cycling hits eccentric/concentric quads hard enough to rupture muscle membranes, spilling massive creatine kinase and myoglobin into the bloodstream days later.
cases.goldenRule: Ease into your first spin or high-intensity class; rock-hard swollen thighs + dark cola-colored urine = go straight to the ER for IV fluids, don't just chug water at home.
cases.episodeTitle: The Pain That Outlasted the Class — First-Session Spin-Class Exertional Rhabdomyolysis — Censored Creatine Kinase (>100,000 U/L), Muscle Transaminase Elevation & Early Hydration/Escalation

cases.title: The Meal and the Match
cases.subtitle: You can eat pasta safely on the couch and jog safely on an empty stomach—combine them within two hours and your immune system pulls the fire alarm.
cases.looksLike: Random unexplained hives and fainting mid-run
cases.actuallyIs: Wheat-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis (WDEIA)
cases.abstract: In cofactor-triggered anaphylaxis, wheat omega-5 gliadin sits harmlessly until exercise, heat, alcohol, or NSAIDs increase gut absorption and mast-cell reactivity, turning a routine jog into anaphylactic shock.
cases.goldenRule: Hives, wheezing, or lightheadedness during exercise after eating deserves an allergist workup and an epinephrine auto-injector—never try to 'run through' itching and dizziness.
cases.episodeTitle: The Meal and the Match — Wheat-Dependent Exercise-Induced Anaphylaxis (WDEIA) Presenting With Dyspnea & Throat Tightness Before Rash — Prompt Epinephrine & Cofactor Traps

cases.title: Struck by a 20-Kilogram Missile With Fins (and the Cold-Water Lung Flood)
cases.subtitle: How an airborne Spanish mackerel caused fatal internal bleeding beneath a 2-cm scratch—plus why cold scuba dives flood healthy lungs.
cases.looksLike: A tiny rib graze you can walk to the bow with
cases.actuallyIs: Diaphragmatic rupture & 950 mL internal bleed
cases.abstract: A 56-year-old angler hit in the flank by a leaping 20-kg mackerel walked to the bow beneath a 7×19 mm skin graze—and died an hour later from silent splenic, pancreatic, and diaphragmatic rupture.
cases.goldenRule: Persistent flank or belly pain after any blunt marine impact—even with barely a bruise—means lie flat and radio MAYDAY immediately for surgical evacuation.
cases.episodeTitle: Surviving Freak Marine Impacts, Diving Edema and Sauna Heat

cases.title: The Eye That Would Not Clear
cases.subtitle: Showering or swimming in reusable contact lenses invites a microscopic tap-water amoeba to set up camp directly inside your cornea.
cases.looksLike: Stubborn pink eye or a dry contact scratch
cases.actuallyIs: Acanthamoeba keratitis mimicking routine conjunctivitis
cases.abstract: Acanthamoeba cysts thrive in ordinary tap water, hot tubs, and pools. Trapped under a contact lens, they burrow into the cornea, causing pain wildly out of proportion to early exam findings and mimicking routine infections for weeks.
cases.goldenRule: Zero water ever touches contact lenses or cases—never shower, swim, or top off solution; severe eye pain + light sensitivity = urgent ophthalmology exam.
cases.episodeTitle: The Eye That Would Not Clear — Reusable Contact-Lens Acanthamoeba Keratitis Diagnosed by Confocal Microscopy — Visual-Acuity Conversion Pitfalls, Water-Exposure Risk & Corneal Preservation

cases.title: After the Flash, One Side Would Not Move
cases.subtitle: Lightning can paralyze limbs and wipe out pulses temporarily (keraunoparalysis)—making living strike victims look dead to rescuers who walk past.
cases.looksLike: A stroke—or a pulseless corpse beyond help
cases.actuallyIs: Transient vascular-spasm paralysis & survivable respiratory arrest
cases.abstract: Charcot's keraunoparalysis freezes limbs cold, pale, and motionless for hours before spontaneous recovery, while lightning-induced respiratory arrest responds dramatically to immediate CPR—the famous 'reverse triage' rule.
cases.goldenRule: Lightning victims carry zero residual charge: touch them safely, prioritize the ones who look motionless and aren't breathing first, and start CPR immediately.
cases.episodeTitle: After the Flash, One Side Would Not Move — Keraunoparalysis (Charcot's Transient Lightning Paralysis) Without External Burns — Intense Catecholamine Vasospasm vs. Stroke & Safe-Shelter Physics

cases.title: Fangs, Stingers & the Painless Bite You Sleep Through
cases.subtitle: Why a single honeybee sting can unmask hidden mastocytosis, and how one nocturnal krait killed three sleeping people without waking them.
cases.looksLike: A fainting spell after a yard sting—or a quiet night on a floor mat
cases.actuallyIs: Indolent systemic mastocytosis / painless neurotoxic envenomation
cases.abstract: Severe drop-blood-pressure anaphylaxis after a bee sting without hives is a classic signature of hidden mast-cell disease. Meanwhile, Asian krait bites feel like mosquito nicks before silently paralyzing breathing hours later.
cases.goldenRule: Epinephrine into the outer thigh first (never delay for Benadryl), get baseline tryptase checked after severe sting collapse, and sleep off the floor under tucked nets in krait country.
cases.episodeTitle: Bee Sting Mastocytosis, Silent Kraits and Travel Myocarditis

cases.title: Paradoxical Undressing & the Heat That Comes Back After Cooling
cases.subtitle: Why freezing hikers strip off their coats—and why community-race runners can rebound into lethal heat stroke after leaving the mist tent.
cases.looksLike: Feeling suddenly warm in snow—or 'cooled off' after a 10K
cases.actuallyIs: Vasoconstriction failure / post-cooling exertional heat-stroke rebound
cases.abstract: Extreme cold exhausts blood-vessel constriction, flooding frozen skin with warm core blood and triggering delusional 'paradoxical undressing.' At the opposite thermal extreme, stopping cooling too soon after exertional heat stroke lets core temperature spike right back up.
cases.goldenRule: Cool exertional heat-stroke victims FIRST via cold-water immersion before transport, and monitor continuously for temperature rebound.
cases.episodeTitle: The Temperature That Came After Cooling — Exertional Heat Stroke After Community Road Races — Why Delayed Tympanic/Oral Readings Miss Lethal Core Hyperthermia & Ice-Water Immersion Physics

cases.title: The One-Finger Fix That Stops a Fatal Bathroom Bleed
cases.subtitle: A 2-millimeter pinhole over an ankle varicose vein can bleed someone to death in under 20 minutes—yet lying flat, lifting the leg, and pressing one finger stops it cold.
cases.looksLike: A messy ankle cut you should walk around looking for towels to wrap
cases.actuallyIs: A high-pressure hydrostatic column emptying through a 2–4 mm pinhole
cases.abstract: Forensic autopsies routinely mistake fatal ankle varicose bleeds for crime scenes because victims sit upright or walk through the house searching for bandages, letting gravity pump blood out of faulty leg valves.
cases.goldenRule: Lie flat immediately, hoist the leg high above your heart, press ONE firm finger directly onto the tiny bleeding dot, and call 911—never walk for towels.
cases.episodeTitle: Plaster Cast Infections, Varicose Bleeds and Medical Air Embolism

cases.title: The Cast That Hid a Flesh-Eating Fire
cases.subtitle: Disproportionate burning pain inside a wrist or leg cast isn't 'normal healing soreness'—it's a surgical countdown.
cases.looksLike: Tight swelling you should numb with painkillers overnight
cases.actuallyIs: Compartment syndrome or necrotizing fasciitis under plaster
cases.abstract: When pain inside a closed cast escalates past what pain meds touch—especially with fever, numbness, or dread—waiting until Monday morning lets infection or pressure race unchecked beneath the fiberglass.
cases.goldenRule: Severe, escalating pain under any cast requires immediate ER evaluation to split/bivalve and inspect bare skin—never sleep it off with stronger pills.
cases.episodeTitle: Plaster Cast Infections, Varicose Bleeds and Medical Air Embolism

cases.title: The Headache After the Birth
cases.subtitle: Childbirth isn't the medical finish line: how a normal blood pressure at discharge and a normal first brain CT still missed a postpartum venous clot.
cases.looksLike: Exhausted new-parent migraine with no fever and a clear plain CT
cases.actuallyIs: Postpartum cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST)
cases.abstract: Ten days after a smooth C-section and normal blood pressure, a 28-year-old developed escalating headache and projectile vomiting—then five seizures on day twelve. A standard noncontrast CT looked normal until dedicated venous imaging caught the clot.
cases.goldenRule: Any worsening postpartum headache unresponsive to OTC painkillers—especially with vomiting, vision changes, or seizures—needs immediate emergency evaluation (and dedicated venous imaging if plain CT is clear).
cases.episodeTitle: The Headache After the Birth — Forensic Pathology, Diagnostic Verification & Real-World Injury/Illness Prevention

cases.title: The Negative Test and the Blood in the Abdomen
cases.subtitle: Why a negative urine pregnancy dipstick cannot slam the door on a ruptured ectopic pregnancy when belly pain and dizziness scream otherwise.
cases.looksLike: Non-pregnancy pelvic cramping because the strip showed one line
cases.actuallyIs: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with internal hemorrhage
cases.abstract: Dilute urine, early/low hCG, or assay hook effects can flip a urine test negative even while an ectopic pregnancy bleeds silently into the pelvis.
cases.goldenRule: Sudden one-sided pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain, or lightheadedness in anyone who could be pregnant requires urgent ER evaluation—regardless of a negative home urine strip.
cases.episodeTitle: The Negative Test and the Blood in the Abdomen — Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy With a Negative Urine Pregnancy Test & Serum Beta-hCG of 10 mIU/mL — Assay Thresholds vs. Worsening Peritoneal Pain

cases.title: The Blood Flow That Did Not Clear the Testicle
cases.subtitle: Color-Doppler ultrasound can still show blood flow during partial or intermittent testicular torsion—right up until the 6-hour salvage window slams shut.
cases.looksLike: Reassuring ultrasound flow you can watch at home
cases.actuallyIs: Incomplete or intermittent torsion strangling the cord
cases.abstract: Preserved arterial flow on an early scan creates dangerous false reassurance when severe sudden scrotal pain and swelling point clinically to torsion.
cases.goldenRule: Sudden severe testicular pain (especially with nausea or waking from sleep) is an immediate ER emergency—return immediately if pain persists or returns after a 'normal' scan.
cases.episodeTitle: The Blood Flow That Did Not Clear the Testicle — Testicular Torsion With Preserved Color-Doppler Flow — Incomplete/Intermittent Cord Twist, High-Resolution Whirlpool Sign & Urgent Surgical Exploration

cases.title: The Fall Beneath the Scalp
cases.subtitle: A minor scalp cut you could staple in ten minutes—hiding a C1 Atlas Jefferson burst fracture at the top of the spine.
cases.looksLike: Just a bumped head with a small scalp laceration
cases.actuallyIs: Occult C1 axial-load burst fracture
cases.abstract: Axial loading straight onto the crown of the head splits the ring of the first cervical vertebra outward—often sparing the spinal cord initially so the patient walks in complaining only of neck stiffness.

cases.title: The Skin Cancer That Never Metastasized—and Still Killed
cases.subtitle: A 2026 forensic autopsy shatters the myth that localized skin cancer is harmless without distant spread, distinguishes sunscreen prevention from treatment, and strips the diagnostic burden off patients.
cases.avoidability: Early symptom evaluation & UV prevention (individual barriers unknown)
cases.looksLike: A stubborn surface scalp sore that can’t be lethal if it hasn’t spread to other organs
cases.actuallyIs: Locally invasive p63+ G2 squamous cell carcinoma chewing through bone and triggering venous sinus and lung clots
cases.abstract: Most people assume skin cancer only turns deadly once it spreads to distant lungs or liver, yet a 2026 forensic case of a 59-year-old man with an untreated scalp squamous cell carcinoma proved zero distant metastases can still end in full-thickness skull erosion and fatal thromboembolism. You do not need to name a changing or bleeding spot yourself—your only job is sounding the alarm early so a clinician can biopsy it.
cases.goldenRule: If a spot on your skin is changing, bleeding, crusting, painful, or refusing to heal, book a clinical exam and biopsy—you are the smoke alarm, not the fire investigator.
cases.episodeTitle: The Lesion That Needed a Name

cases.title: The Headache That Shifted on the Stairs
cases.subtitle: How Cryptococcus neoformans crushed a 22-year-old's brain inward from a lung toruloma, why a '100%' nine-sample lab match drops to 65.5% confidence, and why a diagnosis never freezes the biology.
cases.avoidability: Uncertain (ward treatment ledger absent; early positional-headache & vomiting recognition critical)
cases.looksLike: Two and a half weeks of stubborn dehydration headache with no rash and no stroke signs
cases.actuallyIs: Disseminated Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis crushing the brain inward from a pulmonary toruloma
cases.abstract: An archival University of Adelaide pathology dossier reveals how an inhaled soil fungus built a lung mass and silently crushed a young worker's ventricles inward behind two and a half weeks of positional headache and zero stroke signs. Paired with modern antigen-assay math, the case shows why meningitis is never a symptom bingo card—and why waiting for a bacterial glass-test rash can waste the only window left.
cases.goldenRule: Call emergency services immediately for a severe or movement-worsening headache paired with vomiting, fever, neck stiffness, confusion, or a first seizure—and never wait for a rash.
cases.episodeTitle: The Headache That Needed a Second Question

cases.title: The Aorta That Popped—and the Labs That Refused to Speak
cases.subtitle: How a New Zealand autopsy separated undeniable structural catastrophe from unconfirmed root cause—exposing formalin DNA sabotage, cross-reacting stains, and the shared-power-source probability trap.
cases.avoidability: Uncertain (root etiology unconfirmed; emergency triage for acute tearing chest/back pain critical)
cases.looksLike: A television forensic slam-dunk where DNA and blood panels deliver one clean verdict in ten minutes
cases.actuallyIs: A transmural thoracic aortic aneurysm rupture trapped in an irreducible postmortem assay standoff
cases.abstract: When a 43-year-old woman collapsed from a ruptured 55-mm thoracic aortic aneurysm with classic tree-bark scarring, postmortem serology, immunohistochemistry, and tissue PCR locked into a complete diagnostic standoff. Her case dismantles CSI certainty, explains why you cannot multiply error rates across dependent blood assays, and anchors the only rule that matters during sudden tearing chest pain.
cases.goldenRule: Call 911 immediately for sudden, severe tearing chest, back, or abdominal pain with clammy shock—never debate the root cause—and start CPR plus an AED at once if someone collapses.
cases.episodeTitle: The Tests That Would Not Agree

cases.title: One Placenta, Three Lives, and the Valve That Went One Way
cases.subtitle: Unpacking the hydrodynamics of monochorionic triplet feto-fetal transfusion, the honest 19.0% weight-discordance math, why twin laser trials don't fit 32-week triplets, and what to watch between scans.
cases.avoidability: Uncertain (32-week triplet laser evidence absent; amniotic fluid pocket surveillance & prompt symptom triage critical)
cases.looksLike: A stable 32-week triplet pregnancy cleared by a normal admission Doppler and non-stress test
cases.actuallyIs: Lethal triplet feto-fetal transfusion syndrome across uncompensated deep arteriovenous anastomoses
cases.abstract: A 2017 forensic case of monochorionic triplets lost around 33 weeks after an unremarkable admission Doppler exposes how deep arteriovenous shunts silently overload one fetus while draining two siblings. It reveals why amniotic fluid pockets outrank static snapshots, why textbook 20% cutoffs miss messy physiology, and why home heartbeat kits create deadly false comfort.
cases.goldenRule: Contact your maternity unit immediately for any reduced, absent, or changed fetal movements or sudden abdominal distension—and never use a home Doppler kit to reassure yourself.
cases.episodeTitle: The Placenta They Shared

cases.title: The 9-Centimeter Colon With Textbook Vitals
cases.subtitle: Unpacking a classic diagnostic mirage where a real CT crisis and real C. diff colitis hid an even deeper heme-factory pileup—rescued only by targeted urine PBG/ALA testing and IV hematin.
cases.looksLike: Stubborn constipation—and then a closed-and-shut C. diff infection—under eerily calm vitals
cases.actuallyIs: Acute intermittent porphyria neurovisceral ileus layered directly beneath confirmed C. diff colitis
cases.abstract: When a 22-year-old woman arrived after eight days without a bowel movement and a cecum swollen to 9 cm, her vital signs sat at textbook calm—and treating her confirmed C. diff infection still left her in agony out of proportion to exam. Targeted urine precursor testing unmasked acute intermittent porphyria, proving why one real diagnosis must never erase the second layer underneath.
cases.goldenRule: Seek urgent medical assessment for severe unexplained abdominal pain or inability to pass stool—and if pain persists after scans and infections clear, ask your doctor whether targeted urine PBG, ALA, and creatinine testing fits.
cases.episodeTitle: The Test Beyond the Scan

cases.title: The Five-Inch Lamb Rib Hiding Behind Perfect Blood Work
cases.subtitle: How veterinary surgeons paired a stomach backdoor with live X-ray radar and concurrent endoscopy to save a tiny dog—and why clear breathing never rules out a lethal esophageal blockage.
cases.looksLike: Mild occasional upset stomach in a dog who breathes comfortably and aces routine blood work
cases.actuallyIs: A 120-mm thoracic esophageal lamb-rib impaction racing toward mucosal pressure necrosis
cases.abstract: A 4.18-kg Kaninchen dachshund with a 120-mm scavenged lamb rib jammed across his thoracic esophagus passed both a complete blood count and serum biochemistry without a single abnormal flag. Paired with a 114-dog cohort showing nearly triple the severe esophagitis past 24 hours, his rescue exposes why blood tests miss localized physics and why DIY vomiting turns a scrape into chest sepsis.
cases.goldenRule: Call a veterinarian immediately for suspected bone ingestion, drooling, gagging, or difficulty swallowing even if breathing looks normal—and NEVER induce vomiting with hydrogen peroxide or push it down with bread.
cases.episodeTitle: The Bone That Would Not Pass

cases.title: Therapeutic Level, Normal Liver—and 284 Micromoles of Ammonia in the Brain
cases.subtitle: Unpacking valproate-induced hyperammonemic encephalopathy despite normal LFTs and 'safe' plasma levels—plus the ratio fallacy, why 0-of-12 controls never proves zero risk, and why you never quit seizure pills at home.
cases.looksLike: Routine post-seizure or post-binge fog cleared by normal liver tests, clear CT, and 'therapeutic' drug levels
cases.actuallyIs: Valproate-induced hyperammonemic encephalopathy (VHE) sabotaging hepatic urea-cycle ammonia clearance
cases.abstract: When a 36-year-old man on prescribed valproate arrived acutely confused after an alcohol binge, his CT scan, liver enzymes, and therapeutic drug levels all flashed reassuring green until a single serum ammonia test hit 284 µmol/L. His rapid recovery shows why a therapeutic drug level is never a metabolic safety guarantee—and why abrupt self-withdrawal is just as dangerous as missing the diagnosis.
cases.goldenRule: Call 911 immediately for sudden unexplained confusion, severe lethargy, or behavioral departure from baseline on valproate—ask clinicians to check ammonia even with normal liver labs, and NEVER stop seizure medication on your own.
cases.episodeTitle: The Level That Looked Reassuring

cases.title: The “Healing” Fair Bracelet That Tested at 17,000 ppm Lead
cases.subtitle: How unmarked fairground spacer beads fooled exhausted parents, why chelation couldn't erase cognitive risk in a 780-child trial, and why the FDA warns against teething jewelry twice over.
cases.looksLike: A gentle 'natural' teething bracelet bought at a local fair—or textbook old-house paint in a 1926 home
cases.actuallyIs: Unmarked 17,000-ppm lead spacer beads mouthed by an infant—plus an immediate choking and strangulation hazard
cases.abstract: During a quiet well-child screening in Connecticut, a nine-month-old girl with zero emergency symptoms tested at 41 µg/dL blood lead—traced not to her 1926 home's inaccessible peeling window wells, but to an unmarked artisan teething bracelet whose spacer beads hit 17,000 ppm lead. Paired with the CDC's formal terminology erratum and the 780-child Rogan chelation trial, her dossier proves why prevention beats cleanup and why marketing adjectives never measure chemistry.
cases.goldenRule: Keep all teething jewelry off infants, seal any suspect item with vendor details for public health, and confirm any elevated capillary finger-prick lead screen (≥3.5 µg/dL) with a venous blood draw.
cases.episodeTitle: The Bracelet That Became a Blood Test

cases.title: The Soft Sari Hammock—and Two Normal Brain Scans That Missed Everything
cases.subtitle: How an ordinary indoor fabric hammock drove oxygen saturation to 47%, why blood pressure stays deceptively normal in 'empty delivery trucks,' and the exact first-minute rescue sequence.
cases.looksLike: Harmless soft-fabric indoor play—followed by reassuring blood pressure and two clean head CT scans
cases.actuallyIs: Silent pediatric neck entanglement causing severe hypoxic encephalopathy (SpO₂ 47%) and prolonged neurological impairment
cases.abstract: When a 10-year-old girl became silently entangled in a homemade sari hammock with her feet nearly touching the floor, she arrived with 47% oxygen saturation and severe brainstem posturing—yet normal blood pressure and two spotless head CT scans. Her prolonged altered recovery shatters the illusion that softness equals safety and codifies how to free a suspended child without adding a spinal fracture.
cases.goldenRule: Call emergency services first, support the child's body weight while safely releasing the neck constriction without dropping them, start dispatcher-guided CPR if breathing isn't normal, and remove homemade suspended fabric loops entirely.
cases.episodeTitle: The Hammock That Tightened

cases.title: The Pool With Too Many Watchers—and the Blood That Turned to Acid
cases.subtitle: Drowning is silent, diffusion of responsibility is louder than a lifeguard whistle, and aspirated pool water keeps dismantling lungs hours after a pulse returns.
cases.looksLike: A brightly tiled indoor swimming lesson surrounded by instructors and lifeguards
cases.actuallyIs: A silent hypoxic arrest where diffusion of responsibility blinds the deck and aspirated water rots lungs hours later
cases.abstract: When a 13-year-old boy slipped beneath a public indoor pool during a structured swimming lesson, survival required immediate bystander CPR, 95 continuous minutes of resuscitation, and four days of ECMO after his lungs collapsed hours later in the PICU. His pH 6.67 rescue exposes two deadly water illusions: that crowded facilities watch automatically, and that pulling someone out breathing means the emergency is over.
cases.goldenRule: Reach or throw—never jump in untrained—and if someone is unresponsive out of the water, start CPR with rescue breaths immediately; any cough, drowsiness, or resuscitation demands the ER.
cases.episodeTitle: The Lesson After the Rescue

cases.title: The Toy That Stole Twenty-Seven Volumes From a Toddler’s Gut
cases.subtitle: Engineered to drink water until they seal a pipe shut, these radiolucent spheres hide from X-rays until ultrasound exposes five 3-cm black moons wedged in the ileum.
cases.looksLike: A tiny colorful sensory bead or vase filler—and a toddler who’s still passing gas
cases.actuallyIs: An acid-proof, X-ray-invisible osmotic plug swelling inside the narrowest stretch of small bowel
cases.abstract: After an unwitnessed brush with water beads, a 21-month-old boy developed green bilious vomiting and a swollen abdomen while still passing gas—and a plain X-ray showed severe bowel blockage caused by absolutely nothing visible. Ultrasound finally caught five 3-centimeter water-filled spheres sealing his narrow ileum, revealing why linear dry-bead intuition fails against cubic expansion physics.
cases.goldenRule: If a child may have swallowed a water bead, seek immediate medical evaluation and call Poison Help (1-800-222-1222)—never wait for symptoms, never induce vomiting, and remove water beads from children’s spaces completely.
cases.episodeTitle: The Toy That Kept Growing

cases.title: The Painless Flash You Blamed on the Laser
cases.subtitle: The retina owns zero pain receptors, so it announces a structural tear with silent flashes and tobacco dust—easy to shrug off as routine glare right after a 15-minute clinic procedure.
cases.avoidability: Early tear-to-detachment progression largely preventable with immediate post-symptom dilated exam
cases.looksLike: Harmless post-laser glare or 'just my usual floaters' with zero eye pain
cases.actuallyIs: A rhegmatogenous retinal detachment silently flooding behind the macula
cases.abstract: Immediately after a convenient 15-minute combined Nd:YAG laser session for lens cloudiness and a floater, a 58-year-old highly nearsighted woman reported darkening and a flash of light—yet no exam followed, and seven days later two massive tears had peeled off her central vision. Her salvage surgery and Tanner’s 200-eye study show why painless flashes demand same-day dilated inspection, never a phone-screen self-test.
cases.goldenRule: New flashes, a sudden shower of floaters, or a creeping shadow—even painless and right after an eye procedure—require immediate same-day dilated eye care; never rub the eye or drive yourself.
cases.episodeTitle: The Flash After the Procedure

cases.title: The Floating Uterus That Photobombed an Intestinal X-Ray
cases.subtitle: On plain X-ray it screamed blocked intestine; on dynamic ultrasound it traced straight to the right ovary—a One Medicine clinic in how diagnostic shadows and stoic dogs lie.
cases.avoidability: High (elective spay eliminates typical pyometra; 24-hour triage prevents septic rupture)
cases.looksLike: A wormy stomach bug or blocked intestine with zero fever and barely any discharge
cases.actuallyIs: An emphysematous pyometra inflating one uterine horn toward septic rupture
cases.abstract: When an intact 7-year-old Labrador arrived after one day of vomiting, worms in her stool, and zero fever, radiographs showed a giant gas-filled tube mimicking intestinal ileus beside a normal-looking uterus. Rolling the dog under ultrasound exposed a buoyant, gas-bloated right uterine horn packed with E. coli and streptococci—proving why normal temperatures and sparse discharge never rule out fatal pyometra.
cases.goldenRule: If an intact female dog gets vaguely sick weeks after heat, call the vet immediately with her intact status and last heat date—never press her painful belly or wait for fever or heavy pus.
cases.episodeTitle: The Infection That Looked Like Bowel

cases.title: The Breaking Fever That Hid a Collapsing Spine
cases.subtitle: Antibiotics shut off her systemic alarm, yet inside the bony spinal canal pus kept expanding from T12 to L4 until her legs gave out and her bladder locked shut.
cases.avoidability: Irreversible paralysis largely preventable with immediate symptom-led decompression
cases.looksLike: An infection turning the corner because the fever broke on IV antibiotics—with intact groin sensation
cases.actuallyIs: An expanding T12–L4 spinal epidural abscess mechanically crushing cauda equina nerve roots
cases.abstract: Admitted promptly for a lumbar spinal epidural abscess caused by Group B Streptococcus, a 68-year-old woman watched her fever break on heavy IV ampicillin—just as the walled-off abscess expanded to crush her legs and lock her bladder despite intact saddle sensation. Her emergency decompression and Davis’s 63-case study prove that new loss of motor or bladder function always overrules falling fevers and improving blood tests.
cases.goldenRule: Back pain plus new weakness/numbness in both legs, saddle numbness, or ANY new difficulty starting or emptying your bladder is a 911 spinal emergency—never drive yourself or wait for morning rounds.
cases.episodeTitle: The Fever Was Not the Whole Story

cases.title: Two Back-Pain Pills, Zero Working Drain, and a GCS-8 Coma
cases.subtitle: Small doses only stay small when the exit works: with kidneys offline, just two routine tablets of baclofen pushed a sharp 74-year-old dialysis patient into a coma that shrugged off standard hemodialysis.
cases.looksLike: Expected muscle-relaxer sleepiness—and a clean head CT that can wait until morning dialysis
cases.actuallyIs: Global GABA-B CNS shutdown from trapped renally cleared baclofen requiring emergent ICU clearance
cases.abstract: Twelve hours after taking only two standard doses of baclofen for back pain, a cognitively sharp 74-year-old woman on hemodialysis slipped into a GCS-8 coma with a normal head CT and reactive pupils. Pharmacokinetic studies and a 6,469-patient Ontario dialysis cohort explain why renally cleared drugs overflow a sealed drain—and why severe new drowsiness can never wait until tomorrow’s scheduled dialysis.
cases.goldenRule: With kidney disease, ask before every new pill whether it relies on renal clearance; if severe drowsiness or unresponsiveness hits, call 911 immediately—never wait for the next scheduled dialysis session.
cases.episodeTitle: The New Tablet and the Missing Clearance

cases.title: The Tidy Tonsils Sitting Above a Walnut-Sized Airway Trap
cases.subtitle: Saying 'ahh' only inspects the front hallway; when swallowing tablets fails and a voice turns raspy, the basement airway may be inches from slamming shut.
cases.avoidability: Fatal suffocation largely preventable with functional red-flag escalation and awake specialist airway control
cases.looksLike: A stubborn winter sore throat with clean tonsils, normal oxygen, and zero whistling stridor
cases.actuallyIs: A walnut-sized lingual epiglottic abscess one muscle-relaxation away from total airway occlusion
cases.abstract: Twice discharged for routine 'acute pharyngitis' despite worsening swallowing pain and a raspy voice, a 65-year-old man arrived at an ER looking calm, lying flat, and holding normal oxygen—yet his CRP hit 256.9 mg/L and CT revealed a 28×24×18-mm epiglottic abscess. His awake fiberoptic rescue proves why you never wait for stridor or drooling, and why probing an inflamed throat at home can snap the airway shut.
cases.goldenRule: Rapidly worsening throat pain, inability to swallow pills or saliva, or a new raspy/muffled voice demands 911 immediately—sit upright, never drive yourself, and never press down the tongue to look inside.
cases.episodeTitle: The Throat That Looked Too Ordinary

cases.title: The 135/95 Baby and the Telescoping Gut
cases.subtitle: A 10-month-old arrived sleepy, easily arousable, and hypertensive past the 99th percentile with zero belly tenderness—until an ultrasound caught his bowel swallowing itself.
cases.looksLike: An exhausted baby sleeping off a stubborn two-day stomach bug
cases.actuallyIs: An ischemic ileocolic intussusception driving malignant hypertension past the 99th percentile
cases.abstract: When an infant's intestine telescopes into itself, ischemia can simultaneously flood the brain with sedating endogenous opioids and redline blood pressure into adult stroke territory while leaving the belly completely soft. A 2013 case report and a 141-child cohort dismantle the “classic triad” myth and show why unexplained lethargy alone demands emergency assessment.
cases.goldenRule: Treat unexplained infant lethargy, repeated vomiting, or intermittent crying-then-slumping as an immediate emergency—never wait for bloody stool, never force fluids into a drowsy child, and never poke for an abdominal lump.
cases.episodeTitle: The Sleepiness That Began in the Bowel

cases.title: Fifteen Months of Bladder Pills, Half a Lung Left
cases.subtitle: After 15 months of preventative nitrofurantoin, a woman’s lung volume stayed above 100% predicted while her oxygen-transfer capacity collapsed to 38%.
cases.looksLike: Old asthma or sleep apnea flaring up on a winter afternoon
cases.actuallyIs: Chronic nitrofurantoin-induced organizing pneumonia slashing pulmonary gas transfer to 38%
cases.abstract: Most patients assume drug toxicity arrives within days as a rash or upset stomach, not fifteen months later disguised as worsening breathlessness and falls. A 2020 case report and a 13,421-patient older-adult cohort expose how chronic nitrofurantoin triggers interstitial lung injury—and why a full medication list beats diagnostic anchoring every time.
cases.goldenRule: If new or worsening breathlessness, lingering cough, or faintness hits while taking nitrofurantoin—whether day five or month fifteen—get urgent assessment with your full daily pill list in hand, never self-rechallenge, and stop immediately if clinicians suspect lung toxicity.
cases.episodeTitle: The Breathlessness and the Long Prescription

cases.title: Two Years Later, His Stomach Moved Upstairs
cases.subtitle: Two years after a road crash with a clear abdominal CT, a 57-year-old’s cough and persistent hiccups turned out to be six abdominal organs crowding his left lung.
cases.looksLike: Fifteen days of stubborn bronchitis and annoying hiccups
cases.actuallyIs: A 10 × 8 cm delayed diaphragmatic rupture packing stomach, bowel, spleen, and pancreas into the left chest
cases.abstract: Your chest inhales by creating a vacuum while your belly sits under positive pressure, turning any weakened tear in the diaphragm into a slow-motion elevator for abdominal organs. A 2022 case report and a 40-patient surgical series show why old crashes can resurface up to 21 years later—and why a past reassuring scan never cancels out new breathlessness.
cases.goldenRule: Treat worsening breathlessness, gasping, or hypoxic restlessness as a fresh emergency—tell EMS and triage about any past severe crash or torso trauma immediately, never drive yourself, and never treat an old “clear” CT as permanent armor.
cases.episodeTitle: The Old Injury and the Crowded Chest

cases.title: The Female Cat Who Broke the Blocked-Bladder Stereotype
cases.subtitle: A 10-year-old spayed female cat arrived straining with zero urine output, a dangerously slow heart rate of 140 bpm, and cardiac-arrest-range potassium of 8.9 mmol/L.
cases.looksLike: A slightly plump female cat fighting constipation or a stubborn hairball
cases.actuallyIs: Complete urethral stone obstruction driving creatinine to 15.8 mg/dL and potassium to 8.9 mmol/L
cases.abstract: Because female cats have shorter, wider urethras than males, owners and even exhausted brains often rationalize unproductive litter-box straining as constipation or a hairball. A 2025 case report and the 2025 iCatCare consensus guidelines show how a Corynebacterium-linked struvite stone turned plumbing failure into lethal hyperkalemia—and why effort without urine means immediate veterinary ER triage regardless of sex.
cases.goldenRule: Unproductive straining in the litter box—male OR female, even if you think it looks like constipation—is an immediate veterinary ER emergency: call an open vet clinic directly, keep hands off the belly, and never force water or human painkillers.
cases.episodeTitle: The Blockage in the Less Likely Cat

cases.title: The Toothpick That Walked Out of Her Stomach and Into Her Liver
cases.subtitle: With zero memory of swallowing anything sharp, a 53-year-old’s two-week upper-belly ache ended in a liver resection—and a hidden wooden toothpick inside the specimen.
cases.looksLike: Two weeks of stubborn indigestion with normal vitals and a clear X-ray
cases.actuallyIs: A wooden toothpick perforating the stomach into liver segment 3 and seeding a septic abscess
cases.abstract: When an ingested toothpick aligns vertically inside a soft bite of food, peristalsis can hammer it cleanly out of the stomach and straight into the neighboring liver while the gastric wall heals shut behind it. A 2023 case report exposes why plain X-rays, sterile blood cultures, and a soft abdomen all miss migrating wood—and why grandma’s dry-bread and fizzy-soda tricks make sharp ingestions deadlier.
cases.goldenRule: If you know or suspect you swallowed a sharp object—even with zero pain—get urgent hospital assessment immediately: eat nothing, drink nothing, never induce vomiting, and never chase wood with dry bread or soda.
cases.episodeTitle: The Small Stick and the Persistent Pain

cases.title: Three Clear Visits, a Sodium of 114, and a Bleeding Pea-Sized Gland
cases.subtitle: After three reassuring visits and two normal head CTs for a 12-day postural headache, a young man’s sodium plunged to 114 mmol/L—until contrast MRI caught pituitary apoplexy.
cases.looksLike: A stubborn two-week sinus or tension headache already cleared by CT
cases.actuallyIs: Pituitary apoplexy knocking out cortisol and driving refractory hyponatremia down to 114 mmol/L
cases.abstract: When pituitary apoplexy knocks out cortisol without squeezing the optic nerves, it skips textbook thunderclap pain and blindness and instead masquerades as water-hoarding SIADH that laughs at fluid restriction and 3% saline. A 2026 JCEM Case Reports dispatch proves a clear head CT is a timestamp, not armor—and shows why persistent, position-sensitive headaches demand a second look.
cases.goldenRule: Never treat a past clear head CT as permanent clearance: return promptly if a headache won’t quit or worsens when leaning forward or coughing, call 911/999 for sudden extreme pain, vision loss, or confusion, and never DIY salt-load or water-restrict.
cases.episodeTitle: The Headache That Changed the Chemistry

cases.title: The Barbed Grass Seed Marching Beside His Heart
cases.subtitle: After six weeks of recurrent pericardial tamponade, shock resuscitation, and a “negative” fluid culture, surgeons opened a Labrador’s chest and pulled five barbed grass awns from the sac around his heart.
cases.looksLike: A tired Labrador recovering from “idiopathic” fluid around his heart
cases.actuallyIs: Five migrating grass awns seeding polymicrobial septic pericarditis and cardiac tamponade
cases.abstract: Equipped with microscopic backward-facing barbs engineered to drill into soil, a dry grass awn turns every muscle twitch and breath into a one-way ratchet marching deeper into flesh. A 2024 CASE report exposes why fluid cultures miss tissue-buried infection, why normal Doppler flow cannot rule out cardiac collapse, and why grabbing bathroom tweezers snaps the harpoon tip off inside your pet.
cases.goldenRule: Check paws, toes, ears, and armpits after tall dry grass walks, never dig into swellings or snap embedded seeds with tweezers, and head straight to a veterinary ER if your dog develops labored breathing, collapse, or pale/gray/blue gums.
cases.episodeTitle: The Awn Beside the Heart

cases.title: Two Clinics, One Root, Zero Potassium
cases.subtitle: Two separate clinics prescribed two differently named herbal remedies—never noticing that both hid licorice root potent enough to hijack a kidney enzyme and stop a heart.
cases.looksLike: Harmless herbal tea remedies and tired arms
cases.actuallyIs: Licorice-induced pseudoaldosteronism triggering torsades de pointes, rhabdomyolysis & stroke
cases.abstract: When two clinics separately prescribed Yokukansan and Shakuyakukanzoto, neither noticed both traditional formulas contained licorice root whose metabolite disables the renal 11β-HSD2 enzyme. Unblocked cortisol masqueraded as aldosterone, driving blood potassium to 1.7 mEq/L and triggering pulseless torsades de pointes, rhabdomyolysis, acute heart failure, and an embolic stroke.
cases.goldenRule: Bring every prescription, herbal remedy, supplement, and tea to one pharmacist or clinician—and call 911 immediately for severe weakness, unrelenting palpitations, or sudden speech/face/arm changes.
cases.episodeTitle: The Shared Root in Two Prescriptions

cases.title: The 90%-Quartz Countertop Trap
cases.subtitle: A minor work bump put a completely symptom-free countertop fabricator in front of an X-ray—revealing advanced engineered-stone silicosis that kept scarring his lungs years after he quit.
cases.looksLike: A healthy worker wearing a dust mask in a clean-looking shop
cases.actuallyIs: Progressive massive fibrosis from >90% silica engineered-stone dust
cases.abstract: Engineered quartz countertops pack more than 90% crystalline silica by weight, blasting invisible microscopic shards deep into alveoli where macrophages repeatedly swallow the same indestructible crystal and die. A 47-year-old fabricator with zero cough or breathlessness discovered progressive massive fibrosis only after a minor chest bump—and lost lung capacity for three more years despite leaving the dust.
cases.goldenRule: Never wait for a cough to respect stone dust: demand wet cutting, local exhaust ventilation, and HEPA cleanup—never dry-sweep or use compressed air—and tell your doctor the exact stone you cut.
cases.episodeTitle: The Lungs That Did Not Complain

cases.title: The Ear-Infection Pill That Pulled the Cardiac Brake
cases.subtitle: Following a standard ear-infection antibiotic label to the letter still sent serum potassium to 8.6 mmol/L—because three ordinary drugs locked potassium inside the bloodstream together.
cases.looksLike: Lingering ear-infection fatigue you should sleep off
cases.actuallyIs: BRASH syndrome (K⁺ 8.6 mmol/L, complete AV block & shock)
cases.abstract: A 51-year-old man with baseline renal insufficiency took routine trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for an ear infection alongside his unchanged eplerenone and carvedilol, collapsing a week later with a pulse of 20 bpm, BP 60/30 mmHg, and potassium of 8.6 mmol/L. Normal troponin proved his heart muscle was intact while BRASH syndrome locked his AV node shut—until IV calcium, insulin-dextrose, albuterol, fluids, and empiric hydrocortisone broke the feedback loop without dialysis.
cases.goldenRule: New muscle weakness, faintness, or odd heartbeats days after starting trimethoprim on heart/kidney meds is an immediate 911 emergency—never drive yourself or wait for a smartwatch pulse.
cases.episodeTitle: The New Antibiotic and the Slowing Heart

cases.title: The Overdose Inside the Plastic Tube
cases.subtitle: A blood draw returned a toxic lithium level of 2.05 mmol/L before plunging below 0.10 six hours later—exposing pre-analytical tube contamination and why clinicians must always treat the patient, not the screen.
cases.looksLike: A textbook 2.05 mmol/L lithium overdose demanding dialysis
cases.actuallyIs: Pre-analytical lithium-heparin tube contamination masking real non-lithium sedation
cases.abstract: When a 58-year-old woman on chronic lithium arrived over-sedated and bradycardic after an unidentified ingestion, her first blood draw printed a toxic 2.05 mmol/L lithium level—only to drop below 0.10 mmol/L six hours later because the original sample sat in a lithium-heparin tube. The case proves both sides of diagnostic discipline: a colorimetric analyzer faithfully measures factory-sprayed tube salt, yet unmasking a lab artifact never turns a real clinical emergency harmless.
cases.goldenRule: If severe lithium-toxicity signs hit (confusion, marked drowsiness, slurred speech, worsening tremor), stop taking lithium immediately and seek emergency care—and never assume a new symptom is just a past lab glitch.
cases.episodeTitle: The Lithium That Came From the Tube

cases.title: Drowning on Dry Land After the Lamp Cord
cases.subtitle: Waking up after biting a household electrical cord looks like a close call dodged, yet a sympathetic adrenaline surge can silently drown a puppy's lungs thirty minutes later.
cases.looksLike: A startled puppy who shook off a quick cord zap
cases.actuallyIs: Delayed neurogenic pulmonary edema flooding both lungs
cases.abstract: After chewing an ordinary 110-volt cord, a 3-month-old Labrador Retriever briefly lost consciousness, woke spontaneously, and reached an emergency clinic within 30 minutes—only to crash into cyanosis and 80% oxygen saturation half an hour later despite supplemental oxygen. Neurogenic pulmonary edema floods alveoli from the inside out via catecholamine-driven pressure spikes, proving that scene safety first and rapid veterinary triage beat every home reassurance.
cases.goldenRule: Never touch a shocked pet or live wire until power is safely shut off; once safe, rush straight to an emergency vet even if your dog woke up wagging its tail.
cases.episodeTitle: The Danger After the Puppy Woke

cases.title: 120 Over 70, 98% Oxygen, and a Hole in the Chest
cases.subtitle: A healthy 46-year-old man arrived with perfect blood pressure, 98% oxygen, and zero bloody vomit—yet contrast CT caught swallowed dye pouring straight out of his torn esophagus.
cases.looksLike: A pulled rib muscle after a rough stomach bug
cases.actuallyIs: Full-thickness esophageal rupture (Boerhaave syndrome) & mediastinitis
cases.abstract: When abdominal muscles fire upward against an unrelaxed upper esophageal sphincter, barogenic force can rip a full-thickness hole straight through a healthy esophagus (Boerhaave syndrome) without a single drop of blood in the vomit. A 46-year-old man with no medical history displayed textbook triage numbers—BP 120/70, HR 80, SpO₂ 98%—yet rapid first-hour CT caught leaking contrast and acute mediastinitis in time for lifesaving thoracic repair.
cases.goldenRule: Sudden severe chest pain after vomiting is an immediate 911 emergency even with zero blood, normal smartwatch vitals, or a prior stomach-bug diagnosis—never self-drive or drink water to test swallowing.
cases.episodeTitle: The Chest Pain After the Vomiting

cases.title: The Sore Throat That Boarded the Jugular
cases.subtitle: Five days after acetaminophen temporarily quieted a sore throat, anaerobic bacteria hijacked her internal jugular vein—exposing why normal white counts and oxygen levels never clear a shifting illness.
cases.looksLike: A stubborn viral sore throat on its usual seven-day clock
cases.actuallyIs: Lemierre’s syndrome (septic jugular vein clot seeding lungs & thigh)
cases.abstract: Ten days after an ordinary sore throat temporarily eased by acetaminophen, a 21-year-old woman arrived in the ER with BP 95/58, HR 124, platelets crashed to 27,000/µL, and CRP at 32.84 mg/dL—despite a completely normal white count (7,900/µL), clear lungs, and 98% oxygen. Contrast CT mapped Lemierre's syndrome from tiny 4×4×5 mm throat abscesses to a septic jugular clot, lung emboli, and a thigh abscess caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum, fully cured after a month of targeted antibiotics.
cases.goldenRule: When a sore throat pivots into neck swelling, chest pain, breathlessness, distant pain, or sepsis signs, demand immediate reassessment—and NEVER massage a tender swollen neck.
cases.episodeTitle: The Sore Throat That Reached the Bloodstream

cases.title: The Mushroom That Fired the Wrong Smoke Alarm
cases.subtitle: Why an 87.4% drop in liver enzymes only proves the fire alarm got quieter—not that the house is rebuilt or that the adrenal glands survived.
cases.avoidability: 90–100% (initial exposure) / Lifelong management (adrenal crisis)
cases.looksLike: A dog recovering smoothly from backyard mushroom poisoning because her liver chart is trending down
cases.actuallyIs: Alpha-amanitin acute hepatic necrosis followed by life-threatening Addisonian adrenal failure
cases.abstract: After an unwitnessed backyard mushroom exposure sent her ALT past 13,000 IU/L, a Labrador Retriever walked out of the ICU on Day 8—only to crash on Day 24 with near-normal liver enzymes and flatlined cortisol. This One Medicine case dissects alpha-amanitin necrosis, deceptive lab trends, and why the changing dog always outranks a pretty chart.
cases.goldenRule: Call an emergency vet or animal poison control the instant you suspect wild-mushroom ingestion—and after any recovery, treat returning anorexia or lethargy as a fresh emergency even when liver numbers look better.
cases.episodeTitle: The Illness After the Mushroom

cases.title: The Internal Hemorrhage With a Resting Pulse of 67
cases.subtitle: How legacy clotting tests, calm heart rates, and spotless skin conspire to hide a massive rectus sheath hematoma below the arcuate line.
cases.avoidability: Partially preventable (unavoidable reflex, survivable via rapid triage & medication stewardship)
cases.looksLike: Pulled stomach muscles after a bad chest cold—no bruise, normal pulse, normal clotting screen
cases.actuallyIs: Spontaneous 17.3-cm rectus sheath hematoma dissecting below the arcuate line on apixaban
cases.abstract: With zero fall, zero bruising, a resting pulse of 67 bpm, and a normal aPTT, an 82-year-old man on apixaban arrived in agonizing abdominal pain harboring a 17.3-centimeter rectus sheath hematoma. Learn why coughing tears engorged abdominal-wall vessels, why standard clotting assays miss Factor Xa inhibitors, and why your 'medicine passport' comes first on 911.
cases.goldenRule: Sudden, severe abdominal pain on any blood thinner demands an immediate ambulance—lead with the exact anticoagulant name, never drive yourself, and never press on the belly.
cases.episodeTitle: The Abdominal Pain Without a Wound

cases.title: A Raincoat Against a Mitochondrial Padlock
cases.subtitle: Hydrogen sulfide paralyzes your nose, padlocks cellular oxygen use, and turns improvised confined-space heroics into double fatalities.
cases.looksLike: A routine tank washdown with a wall fan—and later a comforting 96% oxygen clip on a waking survivor
cases.actuallyIs: Acute hydrogen sulfide cellular asphyxiation inside an unmonitored confined space
cases.abstract: Sent into a 28-cubic-meter anaerobic sludge tank in an ordinary raincoat with an undersized wall fan, a 46-year-old worker collapsed in roughly a minute and convulsed for two days despite later printing 96% SpO₂. This forensic audit unpacks cytochrome c oxidase poisoning, table-vs-prose lab friction, and why every confined-space rescue decision belongs outside.
cases.goldenRule: Never enter a tank, pit, or sewer after someone collapses—keep others out, call emergency services from safe air, and never trust your nose to declare the atmosphere clear.
cases.episodeTitle: The Tank After the Collapse

cases.title: The Bellows Under the Anvil
cases.subtitle: Mechanical asphyxia stops chest expansion long before vital organs rupture—turning superficial 'intactness' into a deadly bystander trap.
cases.avoidability: 95–100% (via physical separation & rated load supports)
cases.looksLike: Someone pinned under heavy weight who isn’t bleeding out—so there’s time to hunt for a jack
cases.actuallyIs: Rapid mechanical asphyxia paralyzing thoracic bellows expansion and reversing head-neck venous flow
cases.abstract: Three fatal chest-compression cases involving a truck trailer, an overturned vehicle, and a stone slab prove you can die rapidly with unruptured great vessels and unbruised vital organs when weight locks the ribcage shut. Understand the Boyle’s-law bellows failure, the venous-backflow signs, the morgue denominator trap, and why bystanders must stay out of unstable crush zones.
cases.goldenRule: Entrapment under a vehicle, trailer, or slab IS the immediate 911 emergency—stay out of the unstable load zone, never DIY-jack it, and treat irregular gasps as cardiac arrest.
cases.episodeTitle: The Chest That Could Not Move

cases.title: Sweater Weather Outside, 112°F Behind the Glass
cases.subtitle: How vehicle greenhouse physics, cracked-window myths, and assumed childcare drop-offs turn routine afternoons fatal—and the physical checks that break the chain.
cases.looksLike: A mild sunny afternoon, cracked windows, and an app notification confirming the van completed its route
cases.actuallyIs: Rapid trapped-radiation vehicular hyperthermia and endothelial vascular collapse
cases.abstract: Analyzing a 2017 Malaysian school-van fatality alongside McLaren et al.’s landmark 2005 cabin-heating study exposes two deadly illusions: that mild weather or cracked windows buy safe minutes, and that sweating or a 40.3°C post-resuscitation temperature excludes heatstroke. Learn the exact 911 response, why forcing water can drown a confused child, and why positive human handoffs beat app pings.
cases.goldenRule: Seeing any child alone in a parked car is an instant 911 call—never wait for collapse or dry skin, never force oral drinks, and physically walk every row before locking any vehicle.
cases.episodeTitle: The Van That Was Not Empty

cases.title: When a Human Body Becomes the Drain Plug
cases.subtitle: Why a seizure in water throws out the standard 5-minute waiting rule—and how door swings, drainage, and honest toxicology protect safety without stealing adult dignity.
cases.avoidability: Partially preventable (via drainage, outward-swinging doors & dignified check-in plans)
cases.looksLike: Taking a recommended shower instead of a bath—and assuming a dry-land seizure timer applies if someone falls
cases.actuallyIs: Blocked-drain floor immersion turning an open shower into a closed drowning pool
cases.abstract: A 2019 Japanese forensic report documents how a woman with refractory epilepsy drowned on a bathroom floor when her fallen body covered the shower drain—turning the recommended safer alternative into standing water. Learn why postmortem drug levels cannot prove intentional nonadherence, how Ontario coroner person-years scale real risk, and why any seizure in water demands immediate 911.
cases.goldenRule: A seizure involving water is an immediate 911 emergency—never wait five minutes, never assume stopping shaking means safe breathing, and never clear the person at home.
cases.episodeTitle: The Shower That Became a Pool

cases.title: The Heart Attack Made of Banana
cases.subtitle: Forensic autopsies demolish the 'drunk with a giant steak' myth—and clarify the AHA 2025 five-and-five rescue rhythm.
cases.avoidability: High (via dysphagia evaluation, mealtime handovers & immediate first aid)
cases.looksLike: A diner grabbing their chest silently and collapsing from a sudden heart attack
cases.actuallyIs: Silent complete food airway obstruction ('café coronary') from mistimed swallowing mechanics
cases.abstract: Nine medicolegal 'café coronary' autopsies out of 6,978 cases expose fatal airway blockages from chicken, pasty lunch food, and banana—including a sober stroke survivor and dual-level obstructions contradicting the paper’s own methods. Learn the AHA 2025 5-back-blow / 5-thrust protocol, why blind finger sweeps are banned, and why a wet voice after lunch is a quiet early alarm.
cases.goldenRule: If an eating adult suddenly cannot speak or cough forcefully, call 911 on speaker and alternate 5 sharp back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts—never do a blind finger sweep, and get checked at the ER even after food clears.
cases.episodeTitle: The Meal That Blocked the Airway

cases.title: The Bowel Prep That Handcuffed the Calcium
cases.subtitle: An oral sodium phosphate colonoscopy prep flooded a 15-year-old dog's compromised kidneys, locking up active ionized calcium until his own tremors baked him to 106.1°F.
cases.looksLike: Weakness and shaking from fasting and routine colonoscopy diarrhea
cases.actuallyIs: An acute ionized-calcium collapse, 106.1°F tremor furnace, and osmotic sodium spike
cases.abstract: Hospital waiting rooms trick us into treating medical preparation like clearing a desk before the real work starts. In a 2024 veterinary case report, an oral sodium phosphate bowel prep collided with chronic kidney disease, driving sodium to 168.6 mmol/L, crashing ionized calcium to 0.65 mmol/L, and proving why a normal morning lab sheet becomes historical fiction by afternoon.
cases.goldenRule: If a pet on a procedure prep develops tremors, collapse, blank staring, or labored breathing, call the ER immediately with the original packaging—never wait for the scheduled test and never force water down a compromised throat.
cases.episodeTitle: The Preparation That Changed the Blood

cases.title: The Penny-Sized Part Between Your Bathtub and 230 Volts
cases.subtitle: A forensic autopsy and a police store-bought control charger exposed a fake CE mark, a melted safety gap, and 50 Hz tetanic back spasms fierce enough to crack a lumbar vertebra.
cases.looksLike: Scrolling a charging phone while soaking in a warm bath
cases.actuallyIs: Holding a wet metal bridge wired directly to 230-volt household mains
cases.abstract: We recoil from humming utility towers while casually plugging a lime-sized cube of unverified plastic straight into the same power grid beside a tub of mineral-rich tap water. A German forensic case report traced a fatal bathtub electrocution to a third-party phone charger that swapped a regulated fail-open safety capacitor for a cheap standard part that fused into a solid wire.
cases.goldenRule: Never touch a victim or reach into bathwater when a plugged-in device is present—call emergency services from outside, report electricity and water, and wait for professionals to isolate power before starting CPR.
cases.episodeTitle: The Charger Between the Phone and the Wall

cases.title: Freezing to Death in a Well-Heated Living Room
cases.subtitle: A 78-year-old woman with Parkinson's disease arrived confused and rigid from a heated home with a rectal temperature of 88.9°F, ischemic liver enzymes near twelve times normal, and a monitor full of polite lies.
cases.looksLike: A familiar chronic-illness bad day inside a cozy heated home
cases.actuallyIs: Profound 31.6°C (88.9°F) core hypothermia starving tissues behind 97% SpO₂
cases.abstract: When no blizzard is blowing outside, human intuition deletes hypothermia from the diagnostic menu. A 2026 Cureus case report documented a 78-year-old woman living in a well-heated indoor home whose core temperature fell to 31.6°C behind reassuring vitals, a missing ECG Osborne wave, and a chronic diagnosis that almost camouflaged the crisis.
cases.goldenRule: Never chalk sudden confusion, drowsiness, slurred speech, or worsened stiffness up to 'old age' or a chronic condition—call 911 even in a heated house, cover gently with dry blankets, and never use hot baths or rub cold limbs.
cases.episodeTitle: The Room Was Warm

cases.title: The Autumn Helicopter Seeds That Shut Off a Horse's Engine
cases.subtitle: Hypoglycin A from Acer seeds mimics an inherited genetic fuel-valve failure, sending a Kladruber stallion's creatine kinase to 3,216 times normal while abdominal ultrasounds looked completely serene.
cases.looksLike: Sudden autumn stiffness or mild colic in a horse still willing to eat
cases.actuallyIs: Acquired cellular fuel-valve shutdown pouring 804,101 IU/L of muscle enzyme into the blood
cases.abstract: An idyllic autumn pasture can sabotage equine fatty-acid metabolism without leaving a single lesion on ultrasound. Tracking a surviving Kladruber stallion whose creatine kinase surged to 804,101 IU/L alongside two landmark pasture studies reveals why common tree names deceive, why clear urine on Day 3 lies, and why dried hay can carry invisible toxic seedlings.
